On her third night in the house, the microwave tripped the kitchen breaker, plunging Mara into the particular darkness of a place she didn’t yet know by touch.

She stood barefoot on the cold linoleum, holding a lukewarm bowl of soup, waiting for her eyes to adjust. Moving boxes loomed around her like badly stacked masonry. At thirty-eight, she had finally bought four walls and a roof of her own, and for seventy-two hours she had been quietly terrified that the whole structure was waiting for her to fall asleep so it could shrug her off.

Using her phone as a flashlight, she picked her way down the narrow basement stairs. The house smelled of cedar, damp stone, and the faint, sweet dust of decades belonging to someone else. She found the gray metal breaker box bolted to a stud near the furnace and swung the door open.

Taped to the inside of the steel door was a ruled index card, yellowed at the edges. Someone had written on it in blue ballpoint pen, in neat, slightly slanted capital letters:

*CIRCUIT 4 CARRIES BOTH THE MICROWAVE AND THE TOASTER. DON’T RUN THEM TOGETHER. ALSO, SWITCH 7 IS LABELED “PORCH” BUT ACTUALLY CONTROLS THE OUTLET BEHIND THE BOOKCASE. I NEVER FIXED IT BECAUSE I LIKED KNOWING A SECRET.*

Mara blinked at the card. She flipped Switch 4 back with a crisp mechanical snap, and upstairs, the refrigerator hummed back to life.

The previous owner’s name was Arthur. She knew this only from the closing documents, where his signature had looked like a seismograph needle trying to steady itself—much shakier than the crisp lettering on the index card. The realtor had mentioned, while gesturing vaguely at the crown molding, that Arthur had lived here fifty-one years before his daughter moved him to a smaller place in Ohio with no stairs.

The next morning, Mara found a second card taped to the underside of the kitchen sink, right beside the P-trap.

*THE COLD HANDLE DRIPS IF YOU TURN IT ALL THE WAY SHUT. BACK IT OFF A HAIR. IT WANTS TO BE ASKED, NOT TOLD.*

By the end of the second week, she realized the house was annotated.

She found a card pinned behind the curtain rod in the front parlor, noting that the morning sun in October hits the far wall at such an angle that any painting hung there will fade within five years, so she ought to put a mirror there instead and steal the light for the hallway. She found another wedged inside the doorframe of the mudroom: *SWOLLEN IN JULY. LIFT BY THE BRASS KNOB BEFORE PULLING. DO NOT PLANE IT DOWN OR IT WILL DRAFT IN JANUARY.*

There was one taped inside the medicine cabinet, one beneath the lid of the wooden window seat, and one laminated—actually laminated—and wired to the shutoff valve for the outdoor spigot, detailing the exact week in autumn when the frost first bit the north side of the yard.

At first, Mara treated the cards like a manual. They saved her a plumber’s visit and spared her from ruining a framed lithograph she loved. Slowly, though, the notes began to shift in her mind from instructions to something closer to a portrait.

Arthur had not merely occupied this house; he had been in a half-century conversation with it. He knew the temperament of its hinges, the seasonal moods of its timber, the small ways the earth beneath the foundation sighed during a thaw. One afternoon, scraping old paint off the pantry shelves, she noticed faint pencil marks on the inside of the doorframe—heights, dated in the seventies and eighties, alongside initials she didn’t recognize. Above the highest mark, in that same steady hand, was no index card at all, just a bare reminder written directly on the pine: *She always wore her boots when I measured.*

Mara sat back on her heels and felt a sudden, sharp ache of trespass.

She stopped unpacking. For three days, the paint swatches she had chosen for the living room sat unopened on the counter. The walls were currently a faded, butter-colored yellow she didn’t particularly like, yet the thought of rolling primer over them felt like erasing a sentence someone hadn’t finished speaking. When the fourth stair groaned under her weight at midnight, she froze, wondering if she was stepping on it wrong. She had bought a house to begin a life, and instead she felt like the night watchman at a museum of somebody else’s marriage, somebody else’s winters, somebody else’s carefully tended peace.

On Sunday, rain drummed steadily against the eaves. Restless, Mara climbed into the attic to check for leaks, sweeping her flashlight across rafters and bare floorboards. The space was empty except for a single cardboard box left beside the chimney breast, open at the top.

Inside were old spare tiles, a handful of brass screws, and a battered tin of paste wax. Resting neatly on top was one last index card. Unlike the others, the paper was bright white, the ink fresh, and the handwriting bore the same tremor she had seen on the deed.

*IF YOU MADE IT UP HERE, YOU’RE PROBABLY WORRIED ABOUT THE ROOF. IT’S FINE. THE FLASHING WAS REDONE IN ’19.*

*THE HOUSE WILL TRY TO CONVINCE YOU IT BELONGS TO ME. DON’T LISTEN. HOUSES ARE LOYAL ONLY TO WHOEVER KEEPS THE HEAT ON AND LEAVES THE LIGHTS BURNING LATE.*

*PAINT THE KITCHEN. FIX SWITCH 7. MAKE YOUR OWN CREAKS. IT LIKES THE COMPANY.*

Mara stayed in the attic until the rain softened to a drizzle. Then she carried the card downstairs, propped it on the windowsill above the sink, and turned the cold tap until it stopped dripping—just a hair shy of shut.

She picked up a roller, pried open a can of deep, slate-blue paint, and made the first long stroke across the yellow wall.
